units.title: Greek period study: Relations between Greek states, 492–404 BC

topics.title: The challenge of the Persian Empire, 492–479 BC

subtopics.title: Persian aims and the Greek response

outcomes.text: Explain Persian aims under Darius and Xerxes and Mardonius' expedition of 492 BC.
Describe Marathon, Greek and Persian strategy, and Sparta's response.

subtopics.title: The Hellenic League and the invasion

outcomes.text: Explain medising and the different Greek responses to Persia.
Describe how the Hellenic League formed, who led it, and the debates before Salamis and Plataea.

subtopics.title: Athens, Sparta and the Delian League

outcomes.text: Explain the consequences of victory over Persia for Athens and Sparta.
Describe the growth of Athenian power in the Delian League and Sparta's concerns.
Explain how the earthquake and helot revolt of 465–464 BC affected relations.
Describe the First Peloponnesian War, including Megara's defection, Corinth's role and Tanagra.
Explain the end of conflict with Persia in 449 BC and the Spartan invasion of Attica in 446 BC.

subtopics.title: The Peace of 446 BC and the road to war

outcomes.text: Explain the balance of power under the Peace of 446 BC.
Explain the role of Corinth and Sparta in the revolt of Samos and the causes of war in 431 BC.

subtopics.title: Strategies and the course of the war

outcomes.text: Compare Athenian and Spartan strategies and the effects of invading Attica and the plague.
Explain Pylos and Sphacteria, their effect on Sparta, and Brasidas in Thrace.
Explain differences within Athens and Sparta about peace.
Explain the terms of the Peace of Nicias and why it failed, including allies' refusal and the Spartan-Athenian alliance.

topics.title: The end of the Peloponnesian War, 419–404 BC

outcomes.text: Explain the alliance of Athens, Argos, Mantinea and Elis and the effect of the Battle of Mantinea.
Explain the consequences of the Sicilian Expedition and the occupation of Decelea.
Explain Persia's aims and impact on the final years of the war and relations with Sparta and Athens.
Evaluate historians' views on why the Greeks defeated Persia in 480–479 BC.
Evaluate historians' views on the cause of the Peloponnesian War.
Evaluate historians' views on why Athens failed in the Peloponnesian War.

units.title: Greek depth study: The Society and Politics of Sparta, 478–404 BC

outcomes.text: Describe the organisation and content of the agoge and the education of girls.
Explain the values the agoge was meant to build.
Explain the status, roles and contributions of Spartiates, perioikoi and helots.
Explain how helots affected Spartan policy, including revolts and the krypteia.
Describe the status and role of Spartan women.
Explain the roles of the kings, gerousia, ephors and assembly.
Analyse key Spartan debates, such as on Athenian sea-power and war in 432 BC.
Assess the influence of individuals such as Pausanias, Archidamus, Sthenelaidas and Lysander.
Explain how each social group contributed to the army and how it was organised.
Explain Spartan successes and failures, including Pylos, Thrace and Mantinea.
Describe the Spartan navy and the roles of Brasidas, Gylippus and Lysander.
Explain what Corinth and Athens say about Sparta and the importance of the Peloponnesian League.
Explain constraints on Spartan action, including oliganthropia and slowness to act.
Explain the idea of the Spartan mirage and the quality of the evidence.

units.title: Greek depth study: The Culture and Politics of Athens, c.460–c.399 BC

outcomes.text: Explain democracy and oligarchy and who took part in Athens' democracy.
Explain the ecclesia, boule, archons, strategoi, ostracism and the courts.
Assess critiques of the system and the importance of rhetoric.
Explain how Athens ruled its empire and treated allies.
Assess Pericles, Cleon, Nicias and Alcibiades as leaders.
Describe the roles of citizens, metics, slaves and women.

topics.title: New thinking and ideas in Athens

outcomes.text: Explain the Sophists, their teaching and their views of Athenian society.
Explain Socrates' method, his critique of democracy, and his trial and execution.

topics.title: Art and architecture in Athenian culture

outcomes.text: Explain how the Persian Wars and Delian League funds led to the building programme.
Describe the main Acropolis and Agora buildings, and sites such as Sounion and Brauron.
Interpret the sculpture on the Acropolis.
Explain the City Dionysia and Lenaea festivals.
Explain tragedy and comedy as genres and how comedy engaged with events.
Describe attitudes to religion, the festival calendar and the Panathenaea on the Acropolis.
Explain the roles of Athena and Poseidon.
Explain changing ideas about gods and men, including the Sophists' views.

units.title: Greek depth study: The Rise of Macedon, c.359–323 BC

topics.title: The growth of Macedonian power and Philip

outcomes.text: Explain Philip's opportunism, diplomacy, military reorganisation and court.
Describe the expansion of Macedon and how Philip secured it.
Explain the Peace of Philocrates and Philip's expeditions into Thrace and Greece.
Explain the sieges of Perinthus and Byzantium and the Battle of Chaeronea.
Explain the League of Corinth and Philip's election as hegemon.

topics.title: The major events of Alexander's career

outcomes.text: Explain Alexander's control of Greece and his actions at Troy and Gordium.
Describe the victories at the Granicus, Halicarnassus, Issus and Gaugamela.
Describe the foundation cities and the occupations of Babylon and Persepolis.
Explain the pursuit of Darius and Bessus and the conspiracies against Alexander.
Describe the murder of Cleitus, Callisthenes' opposition, and the marriage to Roxane.
Describe the Indus campaign, the mutiny at the Hyphasis and the Gedrosian Desert crossing.
Describe the purges, Susa marriages, the mutiny at Opis, the Exiles' Decree and Alexander's death.

topics.title: Change and continuity in the aims of Philip and Alexander

outcomes.text: Compare the personal, political, military, economic, exploratory and cultural aims of Philip and Alexander.

topics.title: The character and beliefs of Philip and Alexander

outcomes.text: Analyse Philip's character, diplomacy, attitude to the gods and warfare.
Analyse Alexander's leadership, treatment of others, Persian customs and belief in his own divinity.
Explain the relationship of Philip and Alexander with the Greek states and the army.
Explain Alexander's relationships with Persians and Indus leaders and how sources portray Greeks, Macedonians and Persians.

units.title: Roman period study: The Julio-Claudian Emperors, 31 BC–AD 68

outcomes.text: Explain the presentation of Actium and the settlements of 27 and 23 BC.
Assess Augustus' military achievements and how poetry and coinage depicted him.
Explain the restoration of the Republic and traditional Roman values.
Explain Augustus' religious policy, administrative changes and building programme.
Explain relations with the Senate, Equestrians and people.
Explain the roles of Livia, Agrippa, Tiberius and Germanicus and succession.
Evaluate the Res Gestae and challenges to Augustus' rule.
Assess classical authors' views of Tiberius and his relations with Germanicus and Sejanus.
Explain conspiracies, mutinies, revolts and the treason trials.
Explain Tiberius' religious policy and relations with the Senate, Equestrians and people.
Assess how ancient sources present Gaius' character and the assassination in AD 41.
Explain his religious attitude, administration and relations with the Senate, Equestrians and people.
Explain the accession difficulties and the presentation of the invasion of Britain.
Assess the importance of wives and freedmen and the relationship with Nero and Britannicus.
Explain Claudius' death, administration and relations with the Senate, Equestrians and people.
Assess how ancient sources present Nero and the role of Agrippina.
Explain the Piso conspiracy, the Great Fire accounts of Tacitus and Suetonius, and Corbulo in Armenia.
Explain the revolt of Vindex, Nero's death and Galba's accession.
Explain Nero's religion, administration and relations with the Senate, Equestrians and people.
Evaluate how far Augustus restored the Republic.
Evaluate historians' views of the characters of Tiberius, Gaius, Claudius and Nero.
Evaluate the benefits of imperial rule for the inhabitants of Rome.

units.title: Roman depth study: The Breakdown of the Late Republic, 88–31 BC

outcomes.text: Explain the roles of the Senate, assemblies, magistrates and the cursus honorum.
Explain the role of tribunes and courts, and the problems from the Gracchi and Marius up to 88 BC.
Explain Sulla's reforms and the undoing of them up to Pompey and Crassus in 70 BC.
Explain the Catilinarian Conspiracy, the First Triumvirate and unrest in the 50s BC.
Explain the causes of the Civil War in 49 BC and Caesar's dictatorship.
Explain Caesar's assassination, Antony's conflict with the Senate and the Second Triumvirate.
Explain Octavian's success: unifying Italy, Actium and Egypt.
Explain patron-client relationships, optimates and populares, land bills and largesse.
Explain intimidation, violence, bribery, corruption and oratory.
Explain military commands, army support, political marriages and scandals.
Explain the standing of Senators, Equestrians and publicani.
Explain the changing role of the rural and urban poor and land reform.
Explain inequality, corn doles and Spartacus' slave revolt.

topics.title: Individuals in the breakdown of the Republic

outcomes.text: Assess the roles of Sulla, Pompey, Crassus, Cicero, Catiline and Cato.
Assess the roles of Caesar, Clodius, Brutus, Cassius, Antony, Sextus Pompeius and Octavian.

units.title: Roman depth study: The Flavians, AD 68–96

topics.title: The Year of the Four Emperors, AD 68–69

outcomes.text: Explain why Galba, Otho and Vitellius failed.
Explain how Vespasian gained the principate through military, political, financial and popular support and religious aspects.
Explain the roles of the army, Senate, people and provincials.

subtopics.title: Developing the role of the princeps

outcomes.text: Explain Vespasian's actions and the development of the princeps' role.
Explain how successors changed the principate and its relationship with other government bodies and classes.
Explain the role of family members and supporters.
Explain the main features and character of each emperor's reign.
Explain actions affecting relations with Senators, Equestrians, the people and provincials, including censorship and taxes.
Explain the use of the army and challenges and opposition to each emperor.
Describe how emperors handled challenges in Britain, Germany, the Danube and the East.
Explain how propaganda supported Vespasian's accession and the presentation of each emperor.
Explain use of architecture, art, coins, inscriptions, literature, building projects and entertainment.
Explain traditional Roman religion and emperors' involvement in it.
Explain foreign cults, the imperial family's worship and the imperial cult.

units.title: Roman depth study: Ruling Roman Britain, AD 43–c.128

outcomes.text: Explain relations between Britain and Rome in AD 43 and why Claudius conquered Britain.
Explain military policy under the governors, frontier moves, and Agricola's campaigns.
Explain why Domitian and Trajan pulled back, including the Stanegate system.
Explain the decision to build Hadrian's Wall and its features and functions.
Explain the reasons for British resistance, its nature and effectiveness, including Caratacus.
Explain the causes and consequences of the Boudiccan Revolt and unrest in Brigantia.
Explain Calgacus against Agricola and how Roman writers portrayed British leaders.
Explain the roles of the governor and procurator and why they secured control.
Explain British collaboration and the use of client rulers such as Prasutagus, Cartimandua and Cogidubnus.
Explain the army's role in dealing with unrest, deployment, and Hadrian's Wall.
Explain Roman influence on the British economy, agriculture, trade and roads and the army's impact.
Explain why towns developed, the types of town and their functions.
Explain towns as agents of Romanisation and the emergence of a Romanised elite.
Assess Fishbourne Palace and the extent of Romanisation.
